item.title: I turned off these 4 Android Auto settings, and my daily drives got a whole lot better
item.itunes:title: I turned off these 4 Android Auto settings, and my daily drives got a whole lot better
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Android Auto is essential for everyday navigation, streaming music in the car, and taking calls. It improves not just convenience, but in-car safety as well.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But some default settings can still be a bit more distracting than they should be. Whether it's messages interrupting navigation or the interface getting a bit more cluttered than I'd like, there's always room for improvement. Turns out, Android Auto gives you the tools to make those changes.

I've found that turning off a few of these features makes Android Auto much better suited to how I drive. I'm not losing any features here and still have access to navigation, calls, and all my favorite apps. But the fewer interruptions and more control go a long way towards improving my driving experience. Here are four Android Auto settings that I'd recommend changing the next time you're in your car.

Turn off messaging notifications

I prefer fewer message notifications while driving

My phone is the center of my digital life, which means that it also receives notifications all day long that can be pretty disruptive while driving. Most of these messages don't need an immediate response, but they still pull my attention off the road while I'm driving.

Android Auto can, obviously, display incoming message notifications on the car's screen. While this can be useful in many situations, in my city's stop-and-go traffic, it is more distracting than helpful. I've found it easier to stay focused on the road by turning off the Show Message Notifications setting. Go to Settings on your phone, search for Android Auto, scroll down, and turn off Show Message Notifications.

The obvious trade-off is that I no longer get a message when a notification arrives. But when on the road, that's not a big miss, and I can always open the messaging app and check for incoming texts there when I'm parked.

I turned off these Android Auto features, and my driving experience got so much better

A calmer dashboard changed everything

3
By  Parth Shah

Turn off the conversation chime

Why message alerts interrupt my driving experience

Visual interruptions are one thing, but Android Auto also plays an audible alert anytime a message comes in. To me, this is just as distracting, because it makes me think something needs my attention. Not only that, but these conversation chimes also interrupt when I'm listening to music, a podcast, or an audiobook.

When I say I don't want communication-related interruptions, I mean all kinds. That's why I've also disabled the conversation chime. To change it, just open Android Auto's Settings on your phone and look for the Conversation Chime option under Messaging Settings. Disable it to turn off the alert. The available options may vary depending on your software version.

Turn off automatic music playback

I prefer curating my driving playlist

Music is a huge part of my driving ritual. It involves pulling up the right playlist for the right mood. With autumn coming in, my current rotation includes a selection of Black Metal classics. Android Auto, on the other hand, starts playing whatever was last playing. This could be a random song on YouTube or Spotify.

It's disruptive, but more than that, just plain annoying. I get why some people like the feature. If you just want something to play with when you start your car, it works well enough, but it's not for me.

Disabling automatic playback gives me that choice. Android Auto obviously still lets me open my streaming app of choice, or even a local-music app like Symfonium. I can then select whatever I want to queue up and have it in my car's infotainment system. It's as easy as that. As it turns out, changing the setting is pretty simple.

Open Android Auto's Settings on your phone and scroll to the Start Music Automatically option. Next, toggle it Off. In most cases, that switches off the behavior. If your car still resumes music playback, your infotainment system might have its own music-resume setting you can toggle off.

Turn off taskbar widgets

Why I prefer a less cluttered Android Auto screen

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

Android Auto can display quick controls in the taskbar that let you access media and navigation functions without leaving the app you're in. It's useful, but personally, I prefer a less cluttered interface. More importantly, my car's infotainment system is relatively small compared to the 14-inch or larger displays some cars come with these days.

For me, the taskbar is already enough. It gives you access to apps and other controls, and I rarely need extra widgets. If you don't mind dipping into the app drawer to switch between apps, turning off the Show Taskbar Widgets option can be a good trade-off for a simpler interface. It's a matter of personal preference, of course.

The setting isn't hard to find. Just tap the Show Taskbar Widgets option under Android Auto Settings, and you're good to go. If you miss the widgets, it's easy to get them back.

Customize Android Auto to suit your driving habits

Android Auto's beauty is its flexibility. It's not that I don't appreciate all these features. It's just that they don't fit in with how I use my phone.

Being able to turn off the features I don't like is a big part of why I enjoy using Android Auto. None of these changes will be essential to every driver. But for me, the best setup stays focused on driving, and turning off these options lets me build a setup geared specifically toward that.

item.title: The new MacBook Pro maxes out at $14,549: here's what else you could buy for that
item.itunes:title: The new MacBook Pro maxes out at $14,549: here's what else you could buy for that
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • The maxed MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR hits $14,549.
  • That sum buys 347 Pi 5 kits or 382 WinRAR licenses.
  • You could instead buy a used 2020 Toyota Camry for about $14,000.

So, Apple just revealed a MacBook Pro. It's called the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and if you max out all of its hardware —that's a 16-inch screen with 16 TB of storage, 128 GB of RAM, and an M5 Max chip, in case you're curious — you get an eye-watering bill of $14,549.00.

With that in mind, partly because I am someone who advocates for affordable, usable hardware (and partly because I'm a Linux fanboy), I've done the research and found some other things you can purchase for that amount of money.

382 WinRAR licenses to atone for your sins

I know what you did

Listen, there's no point in playing dumb. We both know that, while WinRAR does have a free trial for 40 days, it's not very strict about it. You can keep using WinRAR after your trial expires; it will occasionally show up at your door with a hat in hand to ask for what it's owed, but you can just slam the door in its face and keep using it.

Well, for the low price of $38 a pop, you can pay off the sins for yourself and 381 others with a huge bundle of WinRAR licenses. Give them out to trick-or-treaters during Halloween. And that's just if you buy them all individually; you can probably strike a bulk deal if you get in contact.

4 reasons you should stop using WinRAR and switch to 7-Zip

7-Zip has multiple benefits over WinRAR

14
By  Megan Ellis

37 Raspberry Pi 5s with 16GB memory and all the accessories

Find a use for them all!

Why buy one big portable computing device when you can buy 37 small portable computing devices? PiShop.us sells the Raspberry Pi 5 with 16GB of memory for a cool $305, and if you check all the extras (including a case, power supply, cooler, a microSD, a Micro-HDMI to HDMI cable, and a beginner's guide so you actually know what you're doing with it), that brings it up to $390. That's just shy of 40 little projects just waiting for you to make, and if you ever need inspiration, we have you covered.

Raspberry Pi 5
CPU
Arm Cortex-A76 (quad-core, 2.4GHz)
Memory
Up to 8GB LPDDR4X SDRAM
Operating System
Raspberry Pi OS (official)
Ports
2× USB 3.0, 2× USB 2.0, Ethernet, 2x micro HDMI, 2× 4-lane MIPI transceivers, PCIe Gen 2.0 interface, USB-C, 40-pin GPIO header
GPU
VideoCore VII
Starting Price
$60

The Raspberry Pi is back, and the fifth iteration of the SBC is a lot more capable than the older models. From a new quad-core Arm Cortex-A76 CPU, support for dual monitor setups at 4K 60Hz, and a dedicated power button, there's a lot to love about this palm-sized computer.

$130 at Adafruit $110 at SparkFun Electronics $110 at CanaKit

A used 2020 Toyota Camry

It looks pretty flashy

Credit: Toyota

I know that $14,549 is car-buying money; however, I'm not a car person, so I have no idea what kind of car it would buy. Fortunately, our good friends over at CarBuzz are all car people, and they pinned a used 2020 Toyota Camry at an estimated price of $14,000. So, your MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display money can score you a used car, gas money, and maybe some nice in-car tech, too.

Apple finally caves and brings an OLED touchscreen to the MacBook Pro

The tech giant has resisted the concept of a touchscreen laptop for years, but not anymore.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: I switched my smart devices to Thread instead of Wi-Fi, and latency disappeared
item.itunes:title: I switched my smart devices to Thread instead of Wi-Fi, and latency disappeared
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When running a Wi-Fi-heavy smart home, there can sometimes be quite significant lag. You will press a wireless wall switch or trigger a motion sensor, only to wait a few seconds for it to actually turn the light on. Treating Wi-Fi as a universal smart home transport layer is fundamentally flawed. Wi-Fi forces low-power microcontrollers to maintain high-overhead TCP/IP connections, handle continuous beacon frames, and fight for airtime against laptops, phones, and 4K streaming boxes. By replacing them with native low-power mesh architecture using Thread and Matter, this doesn't just incrementally improve smart home performance but can get rid of latency altogether.

5 reasons I’d always choose mesh Wi-Fi over a traditional router

When it comes to routers, I’d choose a mesh router every time. Here’s why.

12
By  Cierra Noffke

Wi-Fi isn't ideal for smart homes

It leads to latency

Wi-Fi makes for a terrible standard for basic IoT sensors because of the friction it creates. As a result you get a lot of smart home latency.

Wi-Fi relies on a strict hub-and-spoke star network where every individual endpoint must maintain a direct high-frequency RF link back to the central wireless access point. This can make for a very chatty network. Your router is communicating with countless different IoT devices at once, and as a result this can not only create latency with your smart home devices but actually create latency with your primary devices too.

Every smart bulb and leak sensor talking directly to your main router can clog up the 2.4GHz or 5GHz airtime, creating hidden packet queues and random command spikes.

Alongside this, in order to stay reachable on Wi-Fi, battery-powered sensors must either keep their radios awake (which can drain a coin cell battery in just a few weeks) or deal with heavy DHCP handshakes and association latencies every time they need to transmit a simple motion-detected state change.

Thread is made for smart home devices

Build up your mesh

So why are Thread mesh devices so much better? The Thread/Matter mesh replaces the rigid star layout of Wi-Fi with a resilient self-healing mesh architecture where nodes dynamically route packets for one another. As you add mains-powered nodes, you are physically extending the range, organically transforming your entire house into an interconnected coverage grid rather than relying on a single distant router. It ensures that even far-away devices won't drop out so long as they have nodes to hop to.

Thread and Matter mesh is specifically designed for small discrete control packets, resulting in ultra-low predictable response times. For me personally, it's consistently sub-100ms, which makes a major difference from the three seconds of darkness I have to stand in when I'm waiting for a Wi-Fi smart bulb to respond to my Wi-Fi sensor.

And lastly, the battery life changes pretty dramatically too. Because Thread and Matter mesh devices rely on sleepy end devices that keep their radios completely powered down for 99% of their operational life cycle, this extends the battery life of the device tenfold. It eliminates that constant battery maintenance headache for remote sensors, allowing coin cells and small batteries to run reliably for years without sacrificing responsiveness.

Audit your smart home now

Migrate your devices from Wi-Fi

The best way to migrate over and purge your Wi-Fi clutter is by building a local Thread mesh. In order to do this the first thing you need to do is audit and establish your border router. Deploy a reliable standards-compliant Thread border router connected to your local Ethernet backbone in order to anchor the physical network layer. You have to keep in mind that Thread cannot talk directly to your standard upstream IP network without this translation layer. You need a Thread border router, such as an Apple Homepod, a Google Nest Hub, or a dedicated open-source coordinator, in order to bridge the IPv6 mesh.

item.itunes:title: This self-hosted photo tool replaced Google Photos and OneDrive for me, and it's more private too
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For a long time, like many people, I stored photos I wanted to keep in the cloud. I was more partial to OneDrive, while my wife used Google Photos. Recently, though, thanks to the power of NAS devices and self-hosting we've found a solution that works better for both of us while allowing us to uphold our privacy.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Immich is a self-hosted photo storage and management service, and frankly, it's been nearly perfect ever since we started using it. It combines the modern and simplistic UI of Google Photos with some useful editing and management features, plus a level of privacy that no cloud-based service could offer.

My photos are all organized

Whether it's a timeline or through albums

Right off the bat, Immich presents my photos in the way that I want to see them. Everything in my library is displayed in a timeline, which is basically what you'd expect. pictures are sorted by date, and I can easily jump to a specific point in time thanks to the scroll bar also showing me labels for each year and month. Scrolling is fast, too, and images don't take too long to load as I move down the list, which is nice to see.

At the top of the feed, there's a memories section that highlights pictures taken on the same day in previous years, which is also a neat way to look back on my photos.

Aside from time-based sorting, Immich also lets me create albums with photos of my choosing, so I can easily gather photos from specific events or trips. I use this quite a bit, and the neat thing about them is that they're also easier to share with other users on my Immich instance. While the timeline consists of photos on my own account, I can share albums with my wife and make those photos easily visible to both of us.

How I made my own photo hosting platform with Immich

Ditch Google Photos, iCloud, and OneDrive for this incredible (free!) backup solution.

3
By  Rich Edmonds

There's also the map feature, which lets me see where photos were taken, assuming that information is in the image's metadata. I generally don't use this feature, but if you like building a visualization of the places you've been, this is also cool. It's worth noting that this is all entirely on your local server, so all this information is only accessible to you.

It lets me find duplicates

And there's more, too

In addition to simply being storage for my photos and allowing me to organize them, Immich also ahs various management tools and utilities that help me with other aspects of managing my library. One big example is the duplicate finder, which I used a lot when I was first setting up my library. Immich can find images that look very similar or exactly the same and let you choose which ones to keep, which helps me save my space and keep things looking more organized.

It also has a tool for reviewing large files, so if you have videos or uncompressed assets you don't want taking up a big chunk of storage, you can delete them or compress them if needed.

I mentioned above that the Map feature can also show your photos by location if that information is in the image's metadata, but Immich can lend a hand here, too. The Manage location utility lts you choose a location and then select multiple photos in one go to assign that location to, so even if your camera doesn't embed image metadata, you can easily add it after the fact and create a more complete picture (no pun intended) of the places you've been and where you took photos.

Immich's new automation just killed the scripts I spent months maintaining

Immich now does automation better than the scripts I'd built.

By  Korbin Brown

Finally, another big utility Immich offers is automation. You can create workflows based on certain triggers, such as metadata from an image, or simply uploading a photo, which automatically organize your photos by adding tags or adding them to specific albums. I'll admit this isn't something I've tried in depth, but it looks very capable if this is something you need.

There's even some AI

All running locally, of course

Immich even comes with some AI-powered feature that can also help with organization and finding specific photos. Most notable to me is the fact that it can recognize faces in pictures and identify them as the same person, which makes it easier to find pictures of myself or a specific family member.

I'll admit that it's not always 100% perfect, especially because photos can have lower quality or be at odd angles, but it still works pretty well, and it almost always tags the right people. What's more, if someone is showing up as two different people, I can merge those two profiles into one person, so all the pictures are grouped together and detection improves for them in the future.

Immich is the first self-hosted Google Photos alternative my family actually uses

Immich combines a simple UI with robust image management and backup features, all while running on my local server

5
By  Ayush Pande

AI also enables smart search features, so I can use the search bar to find terms like "garden" or "beach", and pictures of those settings will be returned in the results thanks to image recognition.

All of these capabilities run locally on my server, so again, none of this information is uploaded anywhere on the internet. It just helps me without ever undermining my privacy.

I still keep a cloud backup

But on the cheap

Of course, there's a pretty big problem with storing things exclusively on a home server, and that's the fact that all that data could be compromised by a house fire or other accident that breaks my personal server. That's why I do keep a cloud backup of my Immich files, but not on a service that cares about tracking my data or any kind of information.

My data is backed up to a Backblaze B2 bucket, and I only pay for what I use. Since my backup is just under 200GB, my monthly bill usually comes in at around $1.5 (including tax), which is significantly less than I'd have to pay for 2TB of Google Photos storage, or just 1TB of OneDrive storage. And because Backblaze is not meant for browsing or managing files, there are no AI features or anything that uses my data for training or anything of the kind. It's just a storage service.

I replaced my Google Drive backups with Syncthing, BackBlaze, and TrueNAS Cloud Sync, and it's so much cheaper

It's cheaper, respects my privacy, and is more streamlined

12
By  Nolen Jonker

Immich is wonderful

Many times, moving from the convenience of a cloud service to self-hosting can come with a lot of downsides, but Immich is one of those tools that feels just as good as the real deal. It's got a great UI, plenty of features, and it makes browsing and managing my library feel great. The initial setup can sometimes be a hassle, but I still wholeheartedly recommend it.

Nvidia's RTX Spark platform is out, and we've been spending all our days putting it to the test. It's a powerhouse for local AI, but we've also been testing how well it handles emulating games, playing recent games, and letting a local LLM play Minecraft with us. All of this has been great fun, and could be the shape of our future coverage on new emerging hardware platforms.

But none of this would be useful without the RTX Spark chips inside the laptops or mini PCs that are hitting the market. So, let's take a look at one of those, the new Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1. It's not simply the old Yoga with a new chipset inside, and that makes all the difference.

item.title: Apple finally caves and brings an OLED touchscreen to the MacBook Pro
item.itunes:title: Apple finally caves and brings an OLED touchscreen to the MacBook Pro
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Apple has revealed the OLED MacBook Pro with a ProLED XDR touchscreen, 2,000 nits of brightness, and a 120Hz refresh rate.
  • The laptop brings back the glowing Apple logo, adds an iPhone-like Dynamic Island, and includes six‑speaker audio with deeper bass.
  • The OLED MacBook Pro features Apple's M5 Pro or M5 Max chip and is available in 14-inch/16-inch (starting at $2,900/$3,400).

Confirming rumors that have been swirling for what feels like nearly a decade now, Apple has finally revealed a new MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen.

The new "Pro" laptop features a "ProLED XDR" display, which Apple says is a tandem OLED screen. It features 2,000 nits of brightness, a 120Hz refresh rate, and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. Oh, and it features a touchscreen — suddenly macOS' shift to a more touch-oriented look over the past few years makes way more sense.

Also, in a crowd-pleasing move, the glowing Apple logo on the back of the laptop that the tech giant ditched back in 2016 has returned in all its glory. Other key features include an iPhone-like Dynamic Island that displays Live Activities, replacing the notch on Apple's other MacBook Pro and MacBook Air models.

Interestingly, the new OLED MacBook Pro features Apple's M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, not the M6 chip included in the other MacBook Pro announced earlier this week. Confused yet? Don't worry, you aren't alone. According to earlier reports, Apple may have decided against releasing M6 Pro and M6 Max chips because the performance gains weren't substantial enough to justify releasing them.

The MacBook Pro with a ProLED XDR Display and an M5 Pro starts with a 15-core CPU/16-core GPU, but can go up to an 18-core CPU/20-core GPU, plus 24GB, 36GB, 48GB, 64GB, or 128GB of RAM, depending on the chip configuration. The M5 Max starts with an 18-core CPU/32-core GPU, but can be configured with an 18-core CPU/40-core GPU. RAM options include 36GB, 48GB, 64GB, or 128GB, depending on chip configuration. Storage options range from 1TB all the way up to 16TB, depending on the configuration.

Credit: Apple

The 14-inch OLED MacBook Pro weighs 3lb, while the 16-inch version weighs 4lb. The laptop offers "up to" 24 hours of battery life, so the OLED touchscreen doesn't seem to hit the laptop's battery significantly. Ports include a MagSafe 3 port, a headphone jack, an SD card reader, an HDMI port, and three Thunderbolt 5 ports. Other key specs include Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. The laptop can output to three external displays, or four with the M5 Max version.

Lastly, Apple says that the new MacBook Pro features "six speakers with an all-new woofer design that delivers deeper, richer bass, and updated tweeters for remarkable clarity." All other features, including the OLED MacBook Pro's overall design, seem to be identical to previous MacBook Pro models.

Apple resisted the idea of a touchscreen laptop for years

Microsoft embraced the concept with Windows a long time ago

Credit: Apple

What's most interesting about the expensive MacBook Pro and its ProLED XDR Display is that it features a touchscreen. For years, Apple has resisted the concept of a touchscreen MacBook, with CEO Tim Cook stating back in 2015 that he doesn't think the tablet and the laptop will ever become one device. Apple co-founder Steve Jobs was also notoriously against the idea, calling touchscreen laptops "ergonomically terrible."

We even saw Apple attempt something similar in the past with the 2016 MacBook Pro redesign and the ill-fated Touch Bar. The tech giant eventually ditched the tiny contextual touchscreen with the 2021 MacBook Pro (the company continued selling the 13-inch MacBook Pro with a Touch Bar until 2023). It'll be interesting to see how well macOS Golden Gate handles touchscreen controls. While Microsoft embraced touchscreens when Windows 8 launched, the concept has never really clicked with me on a laptop, and I'll likely feel the same way about macOS — a multi-touch trackpad and a traditional cursor is just a more intuitive way to interact with a laptop.

The OLED MacBook Pro starts at $2,900 for the 14-inch and $3,400 for the 16-inch version. The OLED MacBook is available to pre-order now and releases on November 6th. Earlier this week, Apple revealed the M6-powered MacBook Pro and an iPad Mini refresh with an OLED panel and the A20 Pro chip.

item.title: Nintendo's nightmare gets worse as more Switch 2 games leap to other devices, including Mario Kart World on the iPhone
item.itunes:title: Nintendo's nightmare gets worse as more Switch 2 games leap to other devices, including Mario Kart World on the iPhone
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • A Nxnative fork has reportedly gotten Switch 2 game Mario Kart World running on the iPhone.
  • The Mario Kart World port seems playable but stutters and loads slowly (though the shaders have improved).
  • The Switch 2 game Splatoon Raiders is running on a private Eden build, but it lags and lacks several features.

The Switch and Switch 2 port scene is heating up, with Mario Kart World making its way to iPhone with improved performance and Splatoon Raiders running through a private build of the Switch emulator Eden.

Earlier this week, I covered Nxnative, a Wine-like compatibility layer that lets software written for another platform run on the host operating system — in this case, Switch games running on Mac, iPhone, and iPad (roughly 85 Switch games are already compatible with the tool). The tool also uses high-level emulation (HLE) to recreate Horizon system services and translate Switch graphics operations into Metal (Horizon is the Switch's operating system).

Then, Nxnative was forked to work with the Switch 2 and Mario Kart World. While Nxnative laid most of the groundwork, Will Faust, the developer behind the Mario Kart World port, says the hardest part of the project was getting NVN2 support running (NVN2 is Nintendo's proprietary graphics API for the Switch 2).

While the initial video Faust posted showed off the kart racer title in a messy-looking but still playable state on a Mac, the latest clip shows off the game running with improved shader rendering and a smoother frame rate. This time, the game is also being played on an iPhone, not a Mac. There are still occasional stutters, and Mario Kart World still takes quite some time to load, but it seems even more playable than before and includes on-screen touch controls.

Faust has made it very clear that he has no plans to release the code for this project anywhere, but I wouldn't be surprised if this proof-of-concept inspires other developers to create a public tool similar to Nxnative, but for the Switch 2. Faust has also said the port was created with AI assistance.

Switch 2 game Splatoon Raiders is reportedly running on PC through an emulator

The game isn't exactly playable, though

Along with Faust's follow-up clip, another developer, Sheepish, showed off Splatoon Raiders running on a private build of Eden, an emulator designed for the original Switch. Sheepish says the build was created by compiling source code that was provided to them by another developer.

A brief clip posted to X shows the third-person, ink-filled shooter running and then offers a look at its opening cinematic, which seems to run smoothly. As soon as they reach the character select screen, Splatoon Raiders starts to lag pretty badly, and we don't get to see the title in action. Sheepish says there are "missing implementations" and that the game has no VSync in its current state.

It's also worth noting that, like many similar port projects, Sheepish says they used AI to help develop this build of Eden. Unlike Faust, they mention that the Switch 2-focused build of Eden could be released publicly at some point. A screenshot of Donkey Kong Bananza "recomp" was also recently posted online, though we don't actually see the game running, and the Twitter account behind the post seems relatively shady.

On that note, none of these ports have been verified since there aren't public releases available yet (and there may never be).

item.title: A $3 USB extension cable fixed the Zigbee network I'd blamed on bad sensors for months
item.itunes:title: A $3 USB extension cable fixed the Zigbee network I'd blamed on bad sensors for months
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Sometimes, even when you transfer your entire smart home to a local Zigbee mesh network, you might still have motion sensors going offline, smart buttons requiring five presses to register, and temperature probes dropping off the grid entirely. It's easy to blame cheap hardware, weak batteries, or flaky firmware and then throw money away on replacement sensors, but the real issue isn't always the sensors. It could be electromagnetic interference radiating directly from the server or mini PC hosting the Zigbee USB coordinator. A simple, cheap $3 USB 2.0 extension cable solves a multi-month smart home headache by physically decoupling your radio controller from the silent killer destroying the 2.4 GHz radio frequency spectrum: USB 3.0 interference.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
7 mistakes you need to avoid when setting up your first Zigbee network

Wirelessly connecting your smart home devices sounds great, until it isn't.

4
By  Joe Rice-Jones

What is EMI?

It might be causing your smart home to fall apart

USB 3.0 and 2.4GHz can clash, and this is called EMI, or electromagnetic interference. Intel published the definitive white paper on USB 3.0 radiation spectrums years ago. They concluded that USB 3.0 data lines radiate high-frequency noise around 2.4GHz to 2.5GHz. This means it can directly interfere with any devices on the 2.4GHz spectrum, including, but not exclusively, your Zigbee smart home devices.

Since Zigbee operates strictly on the 2.4GHz ISM band, plugging a sensitive coordinator directly into a blue USB 3.0 port on a mini PC or home server essentially places your radio antenna right next to a miniature microwave emitter of electrical noise. This leads to your packet loss absolutely skyrocketing and your mesh routing tables collapsing.

Essentially, this interference could be causing your smart home to fall apart entirely. It's such an easy issue to miss that you might overlook it and start buying new hardware when you don't even require it.

Switching over to USB 2.0 might be the solution

Get your dongle away from EMI

One of the easiest ways to get rid of this EMI is by switching over to a remote USB 2.0 extension cable. Using a direct USB 3.0 port plug exposes the Zigbee coordinator's sensitive internal antenna to broad-spectrum EMI radiating directly from the host's high-speed data lines. It operates squarely within the 2.4GHz ISM band range, artificially inflating the local noise floor and drowning out weak mesh packets.

Switching to this remote USB 2.0 extension cable physically decouples the radio transceiver from the chassis, moving it outside the immediate radiation zone of the host processor, motherboard traces, and power supplies. You can then restore the ambient baseline radio frequency environment, allowing the coordinator to properly discern actual device packets from electrical hash. This drastically reduces packet corruption and frame retries, eliminating the underlying cause of phantom routing failures.

item.title: My laptop’s NPU sat unused for a year, and I finally found the one local AI job it’s actually good at
item.itunes:title: My laptop’s NPU sat unused for a year, and I finally found the one local AI job it’s actually good at
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've ignored the NPU in my Asus ROG Flow Z13 since the day I unboxed it, and I doubt I'm alone. Task Manager shows it flatlined at 0%, because the Radeon 8060S next to it runs the same LLMs as my PC, and the latest Copilot+ features never gave me a reason to care.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That changed when I finally tried AMD's Lemonade, which now runs FastFlowLM, and Microsoft's Foundry Local, which picks the NPU for some models by default. So I spent a couple of days running chat, transcription, document search, and code autocomplete on it, with the chip's power meters logging along the way. It does work. Just not the way I hoped.

Nvidia RTX Spark takes on AMD Strix Halo, and AMD has reason to worry

The head-start CUDA gives is hard to ignore

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Running your own AI models on the NPU now takes minutes

FastFlowLM, Lemonade, and Foundry Local all reach it without Copilot+

For most of its life, the NPU in my laptop has had little to do beyond Microsoft's own Copilot+ features, and AMD isn't alone, since Nvidia's RTX Spark has an NPU it barely mentions too. FastFlowLM changes that: it's an NPU-first runtime for language, speech, and embedding models, and it now lives under AMD's own ROCm project. Inside Lemonade, it shows up as one more backend next to llama.cpp, alongside AMD's ryzenai-llm runtime and an NPU build of whisper.cpp.

Microsoft's Foundry Local covers the same ground from the other side. On my Z13, it set 11 of its models to run on the NPU by default, including three code-tuned Qwen models. Lemonade alone lists more than 40 FastFlowLM models, and getting either tool running took a couple of commands.

The setup still fought me before I ran a single test

Of course, "a couple of commands" didn't survive contact with reality. Lemonade's catalog entry for the MXFP4 build of gpt-oss-20b downloaded 1.6GB of a 12.1GB model, twice, and then refused to load on either llama.cpp backend. The Q4_K_M build finished downloading all 11GB and then failed to rename the file because another process still had it open, and a second pull fixed it.

Then Lemonade's ROCm backend ran that model on the CPU without saying a word. The GPU's power draw stayed flat, so I only caught it in the logs. Switching llama.cpp to Vulkan put the work on the Radeon 8060S, which is worth knowing if you're setting this up yourself.

My RTX Spark laptop rendered a Blender scene too big for an RTX 5090, and a local LLM on the same machine built it

It's not faster than an RTX 5090, but the additional VRAM makes for some cool tricks.

12
By  Adam Conway

For chatting with a local model, the NPU came last

The iGPU was over five times faster and used well under half the energy

I ran OpenAI's gpt-oss-20b using Lemonade's built-in benchmark, on battery, and logged power from Windows' Energy Meter counters, which report the CPU, GPU, and NPU separately. Then I subtracted the idle draw and worked out how many joules each setup burned per 1,000 generated tokens.

The Radeon 8060S, running llama.cpp over Vulkan, generated 53.8 tokens per second and used about 460 joules per 1,000 tokens. FastFlowLM on the NPU averaged 9.5 tokens per second, and its best run used about 1,200 joules, while its slower runs landed in a gap in the power log. AMD's own ryzenai-llm runtime managed 8.8 tokens per second at 1,700 joules.

Even the CPU beat it, with that ROCm fallback hitting 23.6 tokens per second at 990 joules. The iGPU also started answering in 0.44 seconds, against 4.1 seconds for FastFlowLM, and that's the gap you actually feel in a chat window.

Why the NPU's tiny power draw didn't make it efficient

The power readings show where the energy went. The NPU itself added under 1W under FastFlowLM and 2.4W under ryzenai-llm, but the chip as a whole added 14W to 15W for as long as it was generating. Oddly, most of that extra power didn't show up on the CPU, GPU, or NPU rails at all. The iGPU drew more, around 25W above idle, but it finished five times sooner, so its energy per token came out far lower.​​​​​​​

So a tiny number on the NPU's own power rail doesn't tell you much when the rest of the chip stays powered up for the whole run. Don't expect Task Manager to tell you any of this, either. It showed the NPU at 0% while it was clearly busy, and the GPU at 19% while it generated 54 tokens per second.

Between the two NPU runtimes, there's no clear winner. FastFlowLM's speed swung between 8.1 and 11.8 tokens per second while ryzenai-llm held a steady 8.8, and FastFlowLM's best run used up to 30% less energy.

Transcription is the one job where the NPU earned its place

FastFlowLM kept Whisper on the NPU and left the CPU and GPU alone

Chat is the wrong test for an NPU, and so is coding. That's the usual workflow I use this tablet for, but the NPU is up to the task of transcribing a five-minute voice message. I ran the same clip through FastFlowLM's Whisper model and the NPU build of whisper.cpp, logging power for both.

Whisper.cpp won on paper, finishing in 33.6 seconds (8.9 times faster than real time) for about 450 joules. But the power trace gives it away. The NPU and CPU took turns, with short NPU bursts between stretches of the CPU working at 5W to 8W.

FastFlowLM took 78 seconds, 3.8 times faster than real time, and it stayed on the NPU the entire run. The whole chip added just 8.7W, the CPU barely moved, and the GPU stayed idle. It uses about 50% more energy overall, but at a lower draw, and that's the job an NPU exists for: something that can take its time while your GPU games, renders, or runs a bigger model.

I stopped paying for Otter after setting up local Whisper dictation, and it understands my accent better

Handy replaced my $10-a-month transcription app, and it actually understands how I talk.

2
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Search and autocomplete tripped up in wonderfully weird ways

The NPU embedding model couldn't tell an LED fault from a roasting recipe

Document search was supposed to be another easy win, so I pointed FastFlowLM's embedding model at the 40-page user manual for the AMD Ryzen AI Halo and asked what a slowly blinking blue LED meant. It ran on the NPU without complaint and confidently pulled up pages about SSH settings. Its top four matches all scored between 0.93 and 0.94, and none of them mentioned the LED.

Asked about a blinking LED, the model rated a sentence about the Windows activation key as the closest match, with a recipe for roast vegetables only 0.06 behind. A tiny llama.cpp embedding model ranked the same sentences correctly. In my tests, FastFlowLM's version also returned a different result for the first sentence in a batch than for the same sentence sent on its own.

The fix was adding old-fashioned keyword scoring to the search. With that finding the right pages, qwen3.5-4b on the NPU answered both test questions correctly, with citations, in under seven seconds each.

My local LLM kept thinking in circles, and the fix was downloading a different version of the same model

The wrong quantization turned my local LLM into a circular thinker

2
By  Ayush Pande

My NPU finally has a job, it's just a small one

On my Z13, the NPU lost the chat test to the iGPU. It lost to the CPU too. What it does well is run a job you don't need right now at a low draw, like transcribing a meeting while the CPU and GPU do something more important, as long as you can live with a messier transcript.

The rough edges look fixable, and I'll be retesting when FastFlowLM's embeddings and Foundry Local's completions catch up. If you have a Ryzen AI laptop and record a lot of meetings, FastFlowLM's Whisper is worth a try today.

So a tiny number on the NPU's own power rail doesn't tell you much when the rest of the chip stays powered up for the whole run. Don't expect Task Manager to tell you any of this, either. It showed the NPU at 0% while it was clearly busy, and the GPU at 19% while it generated 54 tokens per second.

Chat is the wrong test for an NPU, and so is coding. That's the usual workflow I use this tablet for, but the NPU is up to the task of transcribing a five-minute voice message. I ran the same clip through FastFlowLM's Whisper model and the NPU build of whisper.cpp, logging power for both.

Handy replaced my $10-a-month transcription app, and it actually understands how I talk.

item.title: An old SATA SSD makes a better Windows boot drive than you'd think, and NVMe barely helps what you do every day
item.itunes:title: An old SATA SSD makes a better Windows boot drive than you'd think, and NVMe barely helps what you do every day
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The question as to whether you need an NVMe drive for booting Windows is as old as the NVMe format itself. Sure, raw speeds are superior with a PCIe NVMe SSD compared to one using the SATA interface, but are you really able to fully capitalize on that advantage with daily use? I'd wager you don't, which is why outside of slightly faster Windows 11 boot times, a SATA SSD is just as good as an NVMe SSD, so long as you go and make a hot beverage while the PC boots up.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Most of your workloads don't require NVMe drives

Unless you regularly deal with lots of data

Most games won't magically load faster because you're using an NVMe drive. In fact, we've tested it and found the actual difference between a SATA and NVMe SSD to be a couple of seconds. That's not dramatic on any level and not worth upgrading if your existing SATA drive is perfectly serviceable. I don't load that many games throughout each day. I may start a title or two, but once it's in RAM, we're largely good to go. Most games won't be able to take advantage of this increased throughput.

The faster speeds you'll see in marketing materials are usually measured in peak sequential speeds. SATA III generally caps out at around 600 MB/s, while PCIe-based SSDs can hit speeds of 15,000 MB/s with the latest generation. Games, Windows as a whole, and software rely on random 4K read/write operations and controller overhead to determine performance. This is where it can get slightly confusing for consumers looking to buy a drive or laptop. The speeds shown aren't usually what you'll fully utilize.

Opening apps, using software like browsers and such, you won't notice much of an improvement. You know what does require high sequential workloads? Moving multi-gigabyte video files and huge backup archives, running massive databases, or editing 4K video content. If you don't do any of that, there's a good chance you won't notice the difference. The same goes for running a SATA SSD as the boot drive for Proxmox in a home lab. I do this with the primary mini PC node, and it's quick enough.

The move from HDDs was the colossal storage leap

The jump from mechanical SATA hard drives to flash-based 2.5-inch and M.2-compatible modules already made a transformative difference to the booting times of an operating system, as well as making the entire OS and its installed games and software feel more responsive. Firing up your favorite flavor of Linux, macOS, or Windows involves much more than simply reading a bunch of files. Mechanical drives utilize spinning platters and moving heads to read and write data.

It works great for long-term data storage, but they simply cannot match what even a SATA SSD offers, usually topping out at anywhere south of 300 MB/s. That's almost 50% of what the interface can handle. The issue back then wasn't SATA vs. NVMe, but rather HDD vs. SSD, and SATA flash storage won that battle long ago. The difference between a 100 MB/s hard drive and a 550 MB/s SATA SSD wasn't simply about throughput. It was also about removing mechanical seek latency and handling small random operations.

PCIe-powered storage is brilliant at what it does, and there are times when having that additional headroom can make a world of difference, but I wouldn't rush out to replace your old SATA SSD.

SATA SSDs are the smartest budget upgrade nobody talks about anymore

They are fast enough for most workloads, and more affordable at high capacities

2
By  Tanveer Singh

Buying new? NVMe makes more sense

The price of SSDs, particularly SATA, is out of this world

If you're building a new PC from scratch or happen to be looking for a replacement drive, I'd go with NVMe or the fastest your budget allows for the desired capacity. PCIe 5.0 SSDs can hit some ridiculous speeds, so much so that you likely won't ever see the drives hit their maximum throughput. Your LAN or some other part within the PC will likely act as a bottleneck beforehand. But if you have an available SATA SSD that's simply collecting dust, it may be time to give it another lease of life.

The issue with buying SATA drives (be it a hard drive or SSD) is that prices are affecting these storage mediums just as much as NVMe. It's why the cost of NAS has skyrocketed because the drives are the most expensive part of the purchase, and yet prices only seem to be increasing thanks to the memory shortage and other strains on existing supply. Like anything within the smart home in 2026, it's always going to be better to reuse something than buy new from a retailer.

More budget PCIe 3.0 or 4.0 SSDs can provide much more bandwidth than SATA without the traditional NVMe tax that would typically be applied across the board. And when it comes to choosing the right PCIe SSD, 3.0 or 4.0 are usually more than enough for most PCs. PCIe 5.0 SSDs are simply a waste of available budget if you won't take advantage of the additional bandwidth.

Make sure the old SATA SSD is still healthy

Just like visiting the doctor for a health check or taking the vehicle in for its planned inspection, SSDs can report on their current status using Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology (SMART). Regularly checking this should be prioritized to ensure your flash-based storage (as well as older HDDs that support it) are operating as designed. The first signs of drive failure can be attributed to some reading reported through SMART.

If you want the latest and greatest in solid-state storage technology, I'm not here to stop you. What I will do is comment on how you likely don't need that fancy new PCIe 5.0 NVMe drive when a perfectly serviceable old SATA SSD is available for installation without spending a penny. And if it's not suitable for your primary desktop PC, why not build a second system or, better still, put together a compact home server and start self-hosting services?

PCIe 5.0 SSDs are the fastest drives I've ever used, yet nothing I do actually got faster

I didn't expect everything to get twice as fast, but I also didn't expect what I got
